title: The Invisible Bottleneck Is Costing You Time You Can’t Get Back - Semiwiki
gist: The 2026 Siemens EDA/Wilson Research study says verification consumes close to half of every IC and FPGA program schedule, but former Intel engineer Joel Jorgensen argues much of that time is workflow defects disguised as verification. Mapping a late NAND post-silicon flow the way a fab maps process flow cut validation cycle time from seven days to 3.5 days and restored a five-week stepping cadence for ten consecutive steppings.

themes.theme: Verification schedule share vs. hidden workflow cost

insights.claim: The 2026 Siemens EDA and Wilson Research Group study finds that verification now consumes close to half the schedule on every IC and FPGA program.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Verification's ~50% schedule share is the anchor statistic behind EDA verification tool spend and emulation capex.
insights.quote: Verification now eats close to half the schedule on every IC and FPGA program.

insights.claim: An unknown share of the time attributed to verification is not actually verification but workflow dysfunction showing up disguised as verification.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: If part of the verification bottleneck is really process waste, buying more tools or licenses may underdeliver versus fixing workflow.
insights.quote: What I don’t know is how much of it is actually verification, and how much of it is something else showing up disguised as verification.

insights.claim: A workflow defect is simply something that didn't go right while the work was happening, such as needing data Tuesday and receiving it Thursday, an upstream team handing down the wrong data, a changed tool nobody knows how to use properly, or a bug report too unclear to debug.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Naming and counting these defects turns diffuse schedule slip into a measurable, addressable cost line.
insights.quote: A workflow defect is simply something that didn’t go right while the work was happening.

insights.claim: Workflow defects exist because of change, increasing complexity and neglect, and unlike product bugs they are rarely fixed permanently so they recur.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Recurring process defects compound as designs grow more complex, eroding engineering capacity that headcount alone cannot restore.
insights.quote: Defects exist in workflows because of change, increasing complexity, and neglect.

insights.claim: Engineering teams design development flows around phases, milestones and integration points like an architect, then start building immediately, a ready-fire-aim pattern that leaves the work itself undesigned.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: The gap between designing products and designing work is where schedule risk hides in every tapeout plan.
insights.quote: We think like an architect, and once we have the outline, we start building the product. Ready, fire, aim.

insights.claim: This class of bottleneck stays invisible because teams never look for it and never design it out the way they design bugs out of a circuit or code, addressing it only after the impact becomes large.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Invisible, unmeasured losses are exactly the kind that persist through cost-cutting cycles and quietly cap throughput.
insights.quote: It stays invisible because we don’t look for it, and we don’t design it out the way we design bugs out of a circuit or code.

insights.claim: The problem of designing workflow defects out is pervasive across every industry and business, is not taught in MBA or engineering programs, and has little published literature behind it.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: A management gap with no standard curriculum is an opening for consultancies and tooling vendors that can codify it.
insights.quote: It isn’t taught in MBA or engineering programs, and not much has been published about designing it out of any industry.

insights.claim: A post-silicon design team on a new NAND device ran three weeks late against a five-week stepping schedule despite long hours, nights and weekends, and its leader could not explain what was taking so long.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Effort and hours are poor predictors of cycle time when the constraint is process structure rather than capability.
insights.quote: We’d been working long hours, some nights and weekends, but I didn’t have a good enough answer. I didn’t know what was taking us so long.

insights.claim: Mapping the design workflow the same way process flow is mapped in a fab revealed that pre-silicon validation flows were too slow for post-silicon: a seven-day full data turn was acceptable when milestones were months apart, but three final validation passes alone consumed 21 days.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Process cadence inherited from an earlier phase is a common, diagnosable cause of late steppings and mask-shop delays.
insights.quote: In pre-silicon, we had months between milestones, so a seven-day cycle time for a full data turn was fine. We ran three validation passes at the end to clean up the design. That’s 21 days right there.

insights.claim: The same factory mapping tool had previously helped deliver a 22-day lead lot when the prior best was 35 days.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Roughly one-third cycle-time reduction from process mapping is a repeatable, capital-free lever on fab and design throughput.
insights.quote: the one that helped us deliver a 22-day lead lot when our best to date was 35 days

themes.theme: Redesigning the work: automation and resource reallocation

insights.claim: Setting a three-day validation-turn target derived from the required five-week stepping cycle, the team landed a 3.5-day validation cycle time, roughly halving it.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Halving a validation turn multiplies the number of steppings possible per year, directly accelerating time to revenue.
insights.quote: eventually landed a workflow with a 3.5-day validation cycle time

insights.claim: The cycle-time reduction came from removing manual review of simulation and silicon data, negotiating the fastest servers from pre-silicon partners, borrowing most of their licenses for the final validation push, and a dozen other changes.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Peak-demand license and compute reallocation is a concrete lever, and it underlines why EDA license pooling and cloud burst capacity get bought.
insights.quote: First: automation, automation, automation. We had to remove manual review of simulation data and silicon data.

insights.claim: After the redesign, the team hit the five-week stepping date like clockwork for the ten steppings that followed.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Workflow fixes produce durable schedule predictability, not a one-off recovery, which is what roadmap commitments depend on.
insights.quote: for the ten steppings after that, we hit the five-week date like clockwork

insights.claim: The team already knew how to do checkout, analog design, logic design, data path design, physical layout and mask-shop database fracture; what they had not done was design the work itself so all of it could fit inside five weeks.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Technical competence is not the scarce input; process design is, which reframes where engineering leverage comes from.
insights.quote: What we hadn’t done was design the work itself so all of that could happen inside five weeks.

insights.claim: Workflow maps of this kind apply far beyond silicon design, having been used across PCB, qual, ASIC design, firmware, packaging, product life cycle, customer engineering, marketing, finance and supply chain.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: A cross-functional method has a larger addressable market than an engineering-only point tool.

insights.claim: Increasing complexity and change are seeping into workflows the same way they are into products, slowing teams down and consuming resources organizations do not have to spare.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: Rising design complexity has a hidden operating-expense tail beyond tool and headcount budgets.
insights.quote: Increasing complexity and change are seeping into our workflows, slowing teams down and consuming resources we don’t have to spare.

insights.claim: The prescribed remedy is to design your work the way engineers design products: intentional, functional, synchronous, with a fast clock.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: A concrete design standard for workflows gives leaders a testable target instead of generic process improvement.
insights.quote: design your work the way engineers design products. Intentional. Functional. Synchronous. With a fast clock.

insights.claim: The author's approach traces to Steven Spear's High Velocity Edge methodology, which he worked to expand beyond Intel's SSD organization during 25 years at Intel, including bringing Spear in to work directly with Intel engineering leadership.
insights.speaker: Joel Jorgensen
insights.so_what: The method has been stress-tested inside a large-scale semiconductor operation, which raises its credibility for other chip organizations.
